purpose: A temporary reservoir for electrical energy. It smooths out voltage dips, filters high-frequency electrical noise, and stabilizes power rails during heavy load spikes so microcontrollers don't crash.

whenToUse.scenario: Decoupling Microcontroller & IC Power Rails (Prevent Glitches)
whenToUse.why: When chips switch internal logic in nanoseconds, they cause tiny micro-dips on VCC. A capacitor right next to the chip supplies instantaneous current, preventing resets.
whenToUse.recommended: 100 nF (code 104) Ceramic Capacitor between VCC and GND

whenToUse.scenario: Bulk Energy Smoothing for Motors, Servos & Wi-Fi Spikes
whenToUse.why: DC motors, servos, and ESP32 Wi-Fi bursts draw sudden 500mA+ surges that collapse battery power rails. A bulk electrolytic capacitor acts like a local water tank to cushion the surge.
whenToUse.recommended: 100 µF to 1000 µF Electrolytic Capacitor across the motor/servo power rail

whenToUse.why: Microcontroller quartz crystals (16 MHz) require matched capacitive loads to oscillate at their exact intended frequency.
Passes vibrating AC sound signals while blocking steady DC bias voltages from reaching amplifiers or headphones.
whenToUse.recommended: 1 µF to 10 µF Electrolytic or Film Capacitor

whenToUse.why: Smooths rectified pulsating DC voltage from AC transformers into steady, flat DC voltage.

basics.title: What a capacitor does
basics.text: It stores a small amount of electric charge, like a tiny bucket that fills and empties very fast. It smooths power dips and filters out noise.

basics.title: Units
basics.text: Capacitance is measured in farads (F), but real parts are tiny: 1 µF = 1000 nF = 1 000 000 pF. Ceramic codes always count in pF.

basics.title: Polarity
basics.text: Electrolytic and tantalum capacitors have a + and − leg and must go the right way round. Ceramic and film capacitors can go either way.

basics.title: Voltage rating
basics.text: Every capacitor has a maximum voltage. Pick one rated well above your circuit, e.g. 16V or 25V for a 5V project.

basics.title: Decoupling
basics.text: A 100 nF (104) ceramic capacitor between VCC and GND, right next to a chip or module, removes fast noise. It is the most used capacitor of all.

basics.title: Stay safe
basics.text: Large capacitors can stay charged after power is off. Never short them with a screwdriver; discharge them through a resistor.

howToRead: The first two digits are the start of the value.
The third digit is how many zeros to add.
The answer is in picofarads (pF). Divide by 1000 for nF, and by 1 000 000 for µF.
A letter after the code is the tolerance, e.g. J = ±5%, K = ±10%.
example: 104 → 10 followed by 4 zeros = 100 000 pF = 100 nF = 0.1 µF.

types.name: Ceramic
types.looks: Small flat disc (yellow, orange or blue) or a tiny blob with two legs.
types.note: Read the 3-digit code. No polarity, so it can go either way round.

types.name: Electrolytic
types.looks: Can-shaped cylinder with a light stripe down one side.
uses: Bulk storage for motors, servos and LED strips
types.note: The stripe with − signs marks the NEGATIVE leg; the longer leg is positive. Put in backwards, it can bulge or burst.

types.name: Film (polyester)
types.looks: Box-shaped, often green, red or yellow, with two legs.
types.note: Very stable and accurate. X2-rated types are made for mains use.

types.name: Tantalum
types.marking: Code like 106 + a stripe at the POSITIVE end
types.looks: Small yellow or orange teardrop, or a tiny block on boards.
types.note: Careful: on tantalum the stripe marks the POSITIVE leg, the opposite of electrolytic. Reversed, it can catch fire.
